entries.name: REINFORCE
entries.definition: A family of stochastic reinforcement-learning update rules that multiply a sampled reward relative to an admissible baseline by the derivative of the log probability of the sampled action or unit output, with a nonnegative learning-rate factor.
entries.identity_notes: This record covers Williams’s REINFORCE update family, including its basic immediate-reward rule and the stated fixed-episode extension. The characteristic eligibility is a score-function derivative. This is not the entire reinforcement-learning task, an action-value bootstrapping rule, PPO’s clipped surrogate, a generic optimizer, or every estimator that uses random perturbations. The acronym names the update structure; no trained policy instance is represented. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 334 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 66 and 66 lines respectively. Match-centered excerpts from all 41 unique hit contents were inspected: ordinary verb reinforce in existing ant/search/pseudo-label records and calculations, plus neighboring Gumbel straight-through discussions and the new gradient-estimator discovery lead, not existing candidate records. Exact checkout counts and differences are retained in the ledger. Ten exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and six full native neighboring records were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The score identity requires valid differentiable probabilities or densities and conditions permitting differentiation of the expectation. Parameter-dependent support or extra direct reward dependence requires additional analysis; a discrete black-box reward need not itself have a derivative with respect to the action.

A baseline that depends on the same sampled action or its current reward does not automatically preserve the unbiased score identity. An input-dependent baseline or a statistic based on past trials can satisfy the stated conditional-independence requirement.
Baseline choice changes variance and can increase it. The mean reward is not generally the minimum-variance baseline, and low variance is not guaranteed simply by naming a baseline.

Expected gradient alignment is not monotonic improvement of each sampled update, a global optimum guarantee, or a convergence theorem for arbitrary step sizes. Zero coordinate rates can prevent movement even at a nonzero gradient.

The original episodic construction assumes a declared finite episode and parameters fixed throughout it. It is not a blanket justification for arbitrary online bootstrapping, truncation, discounting, off-policy sample reuse or action-dependent baselines.

The primary journal paper was read through a public third-party copy and checked against publisher metadata. Only the declared method pages were inspected; its full proof appendix and empirical literature were not independently audited.

claims.statement: For a stochastic unit with conditional mass or density g_i(y_i;w_i,x_i), sample its output y_i, receive scalar reinforcement r and update weight w_ij by alpha_ij*(r-b_ij)*d log(g_i)/d w_ij. The baseline b_ij is conditionally independent of the current unit output given the weights and unit inputs; it may depend on permitted input context or past experience. In the original immediate-reward formulation, the nonnegative rate factor may depend at most on the unit’s parameter vector and trial index; it is not chosen from the current sampled output. Under the stated differentiability and environmental assumptions, the baseline-centered score product estimates the corresponding expected-reward gradient component. A common scalar rate gives an expected update proportional to that gradient; differing nonnegative coordinate rates generally rescale its components and need not preserve collinearity. For a Bernoulli-logistic unit with probability p and input x_j, the eligibility is (y-p)*x_j. In the fixed-length episodic extension, hold parameters fixed during the episode, sum each parameter’s score eligibilities over time, and multiply that sum by terminal reward minus an admissible episode baseline when updating at the end.

entries.name: Straight-through estimator
entries.definition: A surrogate-gradient rule that keeps a hard threshold or sampled binary output in the forward computation while propagating its downstream derivative backward as though the hard operation were the identity function.
entries.identity_notes: The core identity-backward rule is the straight-through estimator named by Bengio, Léonard and Courville, who attribute the preceding idea to Hinton’s 2012 lecture. The paper also discusses a sigmoid-derivative-scaled variant; that scaling is not part of the core identity rule. This concept is distinct from a score-function estimator, a fully smooth forward relaxation, and the separately curated straight-through Gumbel-Softmax estimator with its specific temperature-dependent softmax Jacobian. limitations: This is a biased surrogate, not the ordinary derivative of the hard threshold and not an unbiased estimator of the discrete expected-loss gradient. A usable downstream derivative is required; an arbitrary black-box discrete reward does not provide one automatically.

The surrogate depends on the differentiable extension of the downstream loss between binary states. Equal values at the binary endpoints do not imply equal straight-through updates, and the source’s informal single-layer sign statement is not used as a universal guarantee for arbitrary differentiable losses.

Equation (3) of the inspected paper prints the indicator U>sigmoid(a), but the subsequent proof uses P(h=1)=sigmoid(a). For uniform U, the printed inequality instead gives probability 1-sigmoid(a). This record follows the explicitly used Bernoulli law and discloses the inconsistency rather than treating the printed inequality as verified executable sampling code.

Identity, sigmoid-scaled, clipped and other later straight-through rules require distinct conventions. A generic straight-through label does not establish that their Jacobians, bias or optimization behavior coincide.
The inspected conditional-computation example motivates sparse gating; no universal speedup, accuracy advantage or successful convergence is asserted.

claims.statement: Let a be the pre-threshold or pre-sigmoid activation and h the hard binary value supplied to downstream computation. Compute the downstream derivative dL/dh using that hard forward state. In the backward pass, substitute dL/dh for the gradient with respect to a, as if dh/da were one, and then propagate through the differentiable computation that produced a. In the paper’s Bernoulli-logistic setting, the intended stochastic output law is P(h=1)=sigmoid(a), as used in its proof; the identity backward substitution is separate from that sampling law. Multiplying dL/dh by sigmoid(a)*(1-sigmoid(a)) gives the paper’s discussed scaled alternative, not the same backward rule. No derivative through the actual binary sampling decision is obtained by this substitution.

entries.name: Neural variational inference and learning
entries.definition: A method for jointly training a directed latent-variable model and an amortized stochastic inference network by maximizing a variational log-likelihood bound, using score-function inference gradients with learned baselines and adaptive learning-signal normalization.
entries.identity_notes: This is Mnih and Gregor’s NVIL method, not all variational inference, a particular trained belief network, the wake-sleep recognition update, or the reparameterization-gradient approach used in stochastic gradient variational Bayes. It uses a shared feedforward inference model across observations and does not require a separate optimized set of local variational parameters for every observation. Exact sampling refers to its chosen variational distribution, not automatically to the true posterior. limitations: A sample from Q is exact for Q while posterior inference remains approximate unless Q matches the model posterior. The variational-family capacity and optimization outcome affect the gap to the marginal log likelihood.

Unbiasedness of the raw score estimator and subtraction of a conditionally sample-independent baseline do not automatically certify the final adaptive update. The supplement updates running statistics with the same minibatch before applying them, and normalization changes the update scale. Current-batch centering can introduce finite-sample bias; no blanket unbiasedness claim is made for that full practical procedure.

The input baseline is trained using a squared-signal objective, which the source explicitly distinguishes from maximum variance reduction that accounts for score magnitude. A learned baseline need not improve variance in every setting.

The method needs tractable sampling and evaluation of Q, evaluation of the joint P and differentiable log-probability parameters. It does not require differentiating the sampled discrete latent value, but support, zero probabilities and differentiation-under-expectation conditions still matter.
Local-signal simplifications require the stated conditional independences. Arbitrarily dropping latent-dependent log terms can change the expected gradient.

The variational bound and stochastic gradient formulation do not guarantee global optimization, exact posterior recovery or universally faster inference. Reported dataset comparisons and the complete author implementation are not certified here.

claims.statement: Let P_theta(x,h) be the generative joint model and Q_phi(h|x) an inference-network distribution that can be sampled and evaluated efficiently. For each observed x, maximize the bound E_Q[log P_theta(x,h)-log Q_phi(h|x)]. Draw latent samples from Q. The raw model-gradient estimator averages d log P_theta(x,h)/d theta; the raw inference-gradient estimator averages the learning signal l=log P_theta(x,h)-log Q_phi(h|x) times d log Q_phi(h|x)/d phi. Its score expectation is zero, so baselines independent of the current latent sample conditional on x can be subtracted without changing the raw gradient expectation. The method fits an input-dependent neural baseline and maintains a scalar running center. It also divides the centered signal by max(1,sqrt(v)), where v is a running variance estimate, to adapt the update scale. In the supplement’s concrete minibatch ordering, subtract the input baseline, compute batch signal mean and variance, update the running center and variance using those batch statistics, then form centered/scaled inference updates and baseline updates; the model gradient remains unweighted by this signal. For layered factorizations, local learning signals omit terms that are independent of the relevant sampled descendants under the conditional score expectation, with separate baselines and variance estimates.

claims.statement: Draw independent Gumbel noise and compute y=softmax((log(alpha)+G)/tau) with positive finite weights and tau>0. In the forward pass, use z as the one-hot vector at argmax(y), equivalently argmax(log(alpha)+G). In the backward pass, approximate the derivative of z with respect to its parameters by the derivative of y, while the downstream computation has received z. Thus the downstream gradient evaluated at the hard forward state is multiplied by the relaxed sample’s Jacobian. For log-weight coordinates ell and fixed noise/temperature, that Jacobian has entries y_i(delta_ij−y_j)/tau. Hard output remains one-hot even at large positive temperature, and its categorical sampling law is independent of tau; temperature changes the backward surrogate. This is a deliberately biased surrogate, not the ordinary derivative of the hard argmax or generally the gradient obtained by evaluating the whole loss on y.

The inspected scoring scheme combines a recent-best-time ratio with a dispersion-based correction and a normalized nonlinear squash; it rewards a path relative to local traffic conditions. Data packets sample from a power-reweighted routing table, whereas forward ants also use queue heuristics. Updates are concurrent and local; measured forward times, not recursively bootstrapped estimates from downstream nodes, supply the feedback. Limits: Backward traversal requires bidirectional links; forward and reverse costs need not be equal. The simulation omits full transport-layer error, flow and congestion control, so its comparisons are not deployment guarantees or universal superiority claims. The full-neighbor queue formula uses l_n=1−q_n/sum(q) and weights P_n+alpha*l_n. Zero queue sums and sampling from the restricted unvisited set require a declared normalization/fallback convention. The record does not silently treat the full-neighbor denominator as normalized after exclusions. Zero local traffic also needs a destination-selection convention. Every selected completed route receives positive reinforcement in the baseline, including poorly scored routes; alternatives decrease by normalization. This is not a negative reward on the selected bad route. At r=1 other probabilities become zero, so the algebra alone supplies no permanent full-support guarantee. Positive probabilities remain positive under a finite power reweighting in exact arithmetic; that transformation suppresses rather than categorically forbids rare data routes. The score’s interval is a deliberately rough asymmetric estimate built from adaptive statistics, not a calibrated confidence guarantee. Score parameters, window reset, zero dispersion, denominators, queue behavior and finite precision require declared conventions. Returned information can already be stale under changing traffic. The explicit method and Figure 3 allow good-subpath updates; Section 8.3’s one-destination summary is a simplification. Relations to actor–critic, Monte Carlo and temporal-difference learning are qualified analogies in the paper; the method does not inherit tabular Q-learning convergence or require TD bootstrapping. At each weights update, assign each unlabeled example a one-hot pseudo-target for its argmax predicted class. Treat that chosen target as a label for the update and train the same network on both observed labeled examples and pseudo-labeled examples. The original paper’s Equation15 averages the class-summed supervised loss over the labeled minibatch of size n and separately over the unlabeled minibatch of size n_prime, with multiplier alpha(t) on the latter. The represented original configuration uses independent sigmoid output units and sums binary cross-entropy over classes, as defined in Equation5; it is not silently rewritten as softmax categorical cross-entropy. Equation16 sets alpha(t)=0 before T1, increases it linearly to alpha_f between T1 and T2, and keeps it at alpha_f thereafter. The paper uses Dropout during this training and studies both optional denoising-autoencoder pretraining and training without it. The hard labels are recalculated at each weights update rather than supplied by a separate EMA teacher. The displayed Pseudo-Label rule has no confidence-threshold rejection step. Equations5 and15 use hard pseudo-target loss, while Equation17 defines a different entropy expression. For normalized two-class outputs(0.8,0.2) and pseudo-target(1,0), the class-summed binary cross-entropy is−2log(0.8), whereas the printed entropy is−0.8log(0.8)−0.2log(0.2). Their unequal values refute literal objective equality in this example; this finite algebra does not refute the paper’s qualitative confidence-sharpening motivation. Limits: Wrong hard targets can reinforce early prediction errors; the ramp and low-density-separation motivation do not guarantee target correctness or improved generalization. The original paper’s independent sigmoid outputs need not form a normalized class-probability vector. Its classwise binary loss is distinct from later softmax-based reimplementations. The paper describes equivalence to entropy regularization, but its hard-target loss and printed entropy expression are not algebraically equal. This record preserves the shared low-entropy motivation without asserting objective equality. Specific ramp endpoints, final weight, network widths, Dropout rates and pretraining schedules are reported experimental choices, not universal constants. The paper does not specify an argmax tie-breaking policy. The inspected primary paper is a public third-party-hosted copy with an exact hash. Title, author and workshop identity agree with the indexed original and author-linked citation; original-host byte equality and an exact revision date were not established.

Create one cluster for each finite-domain variable and one label node per possible value, with exactly one active label per cluster. In the binary formulation, incompatible label pairs have inhibitory connections initially weighted −1; a label input sums the weights from currently active connected labels. A cluster activates a label of maximal input, breaking ties randomly. These updates need not be strict improvements. The described parallel implementation is explicitly not exactly synchronous, and the reported simulator selects variables sequentially. When an update cycle leaves the assignment unchanged, terminate if all active-label inputs are zero; otherwise reinforce violated connections, using W_new=W−V_i*V_j in the binary case. The extension represents higher-order constraints by constraint nodes with fixed label-to-constraint inputs and adaptive inhibitory outputs to labels. For a violated general constraint, all its outgoing connection weights are decremented according to Equation5; this must not be silently replaced by the binary active-endpoint rule. The paper defines distinct output functions for forbidden tuples and atmost constraints. Limits: The source explicitly says GENET is not complete: learning may create other local minima. It supplies no guarantee of finding a satisfying assignment or proving unsatisfiability within a finite budget. Exactly synchronous updates can oscillate; the source footnote excludes that interpretation of the parallel pseudocode. Ties can change assignments without strict objective improvement, distinguishing this mechanism from the strict hill-climbing record. The 1994 experiments use a sequential C++ simulation. Proposed speedups from future VLSI implementations are expectations, not measured hardware results curated here. The GENET2 conflicted-variable variant is not silently treated as the default variable-selection rule. General-constraint output functions and representations require care. At an atmost bound, activation in the same variable cluster must account for all participating values; independently inhibiting each inactive value can introduce a false penalty. No numerical benchmark result is curated.

For each unlabeled input, compute one weakly augmented current-model probability vector q. Adjust it to Normalize(q*p_prior/p_running), componentwise, using an estimated class prior and a running average of predictions on unlabeled inputs; then sharpen by a positive inverse temperature and normalize again. Hold guessed targets fixed during student differentiation. Construct one strong labeled view and K strong plus one weak view per unlabeled input, assigning its guessed target to all those views. Shuffle the combined labeled/unlabeled pair pool and use the MixMatch-style MixUp routine: a symmetric-Beta coefficient is replaced by max(lambda,1−lambda), and the same coefficient mixes input and target. Train mixed labeled and mixed unlabeled branches with cross-entropy. Also train against the guessed target on the first unmixed strong unlabeled view and apply a four-class rotation-prediction loss on that view, with the paper sampling 0,90,180,270-degree rotations uniformly. Equations3–4 write four weighted sums; the inspected author implementation instead averages each branch before applying its weights, so numerical coefficients must be interpreted with that normalization. The implementation detaches guesses, stabilizes the prior ratio with 1e-6, and uses a rolling prediction buffer. Its CTA entrypoint selects the first weak view as anchor; the standalone no-CTA entrypoint’s default swapped-view configuration is a different option. Parameter EMA is used for evaluation, not as the guessed-label teacher. Limits: The ideal ratio requires defined denominators and a nonzero normalization total; the inspected code adds epsilon. A poorly estimated or mismatched class prior can distort pseudo-targets. Per-example distribution rescaling encourages class-prior alignment but does not impose an exact equality of aggregate predictions and the prior. This follows from the normalization formula and is checked by a finite curator example. The source calls the input-output information objective fair in a class-balance sense; this is not a social-fairness guarantee. Sharpening may reinforce wrong guesses and does not resolve tied maxima into a unique class. The paper and implementation differ in sum-versus-mean loss normalization and rotation sampling: code assigns rotations by batch quarters.
